transcript.text: Indesit dryer making a horrible squealing noise when it starts up, goes away after a few mins. Still dries fine

1. The jockey (idler) pulley. It's a small spring-loaded wheel that keeps the drive belt tight. When its bearing dries out or wears, it squeals from cold, then often quietens as it warms and loosens up. This is the classic cause.
2. A glazed or worn drive belt. A belt that has gone shiny and hard can slip and squeal on start-up, when the drum is getting a full load moving, and then settle down.
3. Less likely: a drum support roller or the rear drum bearing/bush. These usually give more of a rumble, thump or grinding than a clean squeal. 1. Empty the drum and turn it slowly by hand in both directions. If it squeaks or feels rough as you turn it, that points to the rollers or the drum bearing. If it turns smoothly and quietly, the drive side (jockey pulley or belt) is more likely, because turning by hand puts little load on those.
2. Have a quick look round the drum lifters, door seal and lint filter slot for anything caught, like a hair grip or underwire. This isn't the usual cause of a squeal, but it's quick to rule out.
3. Next time you start it from cold, listen to where the noise comes from. A squeal from low down at the back or underneath fits the jockey pulley and motor area. A slapping or slipping sound along with it fits the belt. If the drum turns cleanly by hand and nothing is caught, the jockey pulley is the strongest suspect, with the belt second. Both are normally replaced together, since they wear as a pair. It's a reasonable job for a handy owner who's comfortable taking the back or front panel off with the dryer unplugged. An engineer can also do it quickly and fairly cheaply. It isn't urgent while it still dries well. Don't leave it too long, though: a failing pulley can eventually let the belt snap or jump off, and then the drum stops turning. It's also worth putting your full model number into Indesit's online safety recall checker, as some older Indesit-group dryers were part of a fire-safety modification programme. When you turn the drum by hand, is it smooth and quiet, or does it squeak or feel rough?
I turned it by hand with the power off and it turns, but there's a slight squeak/scrape and it feels a little rough. Nothing stuck in the door seal or filter that I could find.

That changes the picture a bit. A squeak or scrape with some roughness when you turn the drum gently by hand points more towards the parts that carry the drum's weight than towards the belt slipping. A slipping belt wouldn't show up at hand speed. In order, the most likely causes now are: 1. Drum support rollers. These are small wheels the drum rides on, and they go dry and worn with age. They typically squeal from cold and quieten as they warm up, which fits what you're hearing well.
2. The rear drum bearing/bush, or the felt seal and slides at the front of the drum. These give more of a scraping, rough feel, sometimes with a bit of drum play or black or brown dust around the door opening.
3. The jockey pulley is still possible. Turning the drum by hand also turns the belt, pulley and motor, so a dry pulley bearing can squeak too. It's just less specific than a roller. Two quick checks, with the dryer unplugged and empty, will help separate these: 1. Turn the drum slowly and put your ear close to the front, near the door, and then to the back. A noise from the front fits the front rollers or the felt and slides. A noise from the back fits the rear rollers, the rear bearing or the pulley area.
2. Hold the front lip of the drum and gently lift it up and down, then try to move it side to side. A clunk or noticeable play points to a worn bearing/bush or worn front slides rather than just dry rollers. Also look for fine dark dust or bits of felt round the door seal, which suggests worn front felt. If you're comfortable taking the back panel off with it unplugged, there's a check that settles it fully. Slip the belt off the pulley, then spin each roller and the jockey pulley on its own, and turn the drum without the belt. The part that feels rough or squeaks is your culprit. If you'd rather not dismantle it, an engineer can find it quickly, and these are normally inexpensive parts. It's still fine to use while it dries well. If the noise turns into a grinding, a thump, or the drum starts to drag, stop and get it looked at. Where does the noise seem to come from when you turn it, and is there any play when you lift the front of the drum?

Hard to say where it comes from, sort of lower down at the front or back. I don't know how to check for play when lifting the front of the drum, and I can't tilt it with my bad back, so I'm not sure I can do much more than listen.

The play check doesn't involve tilting the dryer at all. With it unplugged and the door open, reach into the drum, hook your fingertips under the front rim at the bottom and lift gently, then push it gently side to side. A tiny bit of give is normal. A clunk, or more than a few millimetres of movement, would point to worn front slides or a worn rear bearing. It does mean bending and reaching in, though, so please skip it if it's going to hurt your back. It's helpful but not essential. On what you've found so far, my best guess (moderately sure) is:
1. Drum support rollers. A slight squeak or scrape with a rough feel when you turn the drum by hand, plus squealing from cold that fades as it warms, fits dry or worn rollers well. A noise from low down fits too.
2. The jockey pulley, a close second. It also turns when you move the drum by hand, so it can't be ruled out from here.
3. Less likely: worn front felt and slides, or the rear drum bearing. You can still help narrow it down just by listening, with no lifting. Next time it starts from cold:
1. A steady, continuous high squeal that doesn't change with the drum's rotation leans towards the jockey pulley.
2. A squeak or scrape that comes and goes once per drum turn leans towards a roller or the felt. Telling these parts apart for certain means taking a panel off and spinning each one separately. Since dismantling isn't practical for you, an engineer is the sensible route. It's a quick job for them. Rollers, belt and pulley are inexpensive and often done together, so it's normally well worth repairing rather than replacing the dryer. It's fine to keep using it while it dries well. Stop and get it seen sooner if the noise becomes a grinding or thumping, you notice a burning smell, or the drum starts to drag or stall.
